Advanced Math: Systems of equations in two variables
Problem-Solving and Data Analysis: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
Inference from sample statistics and margin of error

questions.passage: Urban beekeeping has grown rapidly over the past decade. Cities such as Paris and Toronto now host thousands of hives on rooftops and in parks. Proponents argue that city bees often thrive because urban gardens offer a wide variety of flowers throughout the growing season, whereas bees in farming regions may face vast fields planted with a single crop.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Beekeeping in farming regions is declining because farms grow only one crop.
Urban beekeeping has expanded, in part because cities can offer bees a varied food supply.
Paris and Toronto have the largest bee populations of any cities in the world.
Bees kept in cities produce more honey than bees kept in the countryside.
questions.explanation: The text's first sentence introduces the growth of urban beekeeping, and the rest explains one reason for it: cities offer varied flowers. Choice B captures both. A overstates a comparison the text only hints at, C is not supported (the text says "thousands of hives," not the largest populations), and D is never claimed.

questions.passage: A researcher hypothesizes that people retain information better when they read it on paper than when they read the same material on a screen.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researcher's hypothesis?
choices: Participants who read a passage on paper recalled more details in a later test than participants who read the same passage on a screen.
Participants reported that reading on paper felt more comfortable than reading on a screen.
Participants finished reading the passage more quickly on a screen than on paper.
Participants who read on a screen said afterward that they would have preferred paper.
questions.explanation: The hypothesis is about retention. Only choice A measures retention directly (recall on a later test) and compares the two formats. B and D are about preference, and C is about speed; none of those show that information was retained better.

questions.passage: Some historians have argued that the printing press caused a sudden rise in literacy in fifteenth-century Europe. Yet surviving records show that reading instruction remained rare for decades after presses appeared, and that most early printed books were purchased by institutions rather than by individuals. Taken together, these records suggest that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the printing press was adopted across Europe more slowly than historians have assumed.
the spread of literacy depended on factors beyond the availability of printed books.
institutions, not individuals, were the primary producers of early printed books.
reading instruction became widespread as soon as printed books became affordable.
questions.explanation: The evidence (instruction stayed rare; books went to institutions) undercuts the idea that presses alone drove literacy, which points to B. A is about the pace of adoption, which the text does not address. C confuses buyers with producers. D contradicts the text, which says instruction remained rare.

questions.passage: The committee's decision was far from ______: members debated for hours before reaching a narrow majority.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: A "narrow majority" after hours of debate means the members did not all agree, so the decision was far from unanimous. "Deliberate" would actually fit a long debate, and nothing in the text concerns whether the decision was temporary or predictable.

questions.passage: Marine biologist Ana Ruiz spent three summers tagging sea turtles off the coast of Costa Rica. Her team's data revealed that the turtles returned to the same nesting beach each year with remarkable precision. Ruiz now hopes to determine how the animals navigate across thousands of miles of open ocean.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It presents a question raised by the findings described earlier in the text.
It summarizes the method the team used to gather its data.
It challenges the accuracy of the team's data.
It explains why the turtles prefer one particular beach.
questions.explanation: Sentences one and two describe the method and the finding; sentence three turns to what Ruiz wants to find out next, a question that the finding (precise return) raises. It does not summarize method (B), doubt the data (C), or explain the preference (D).

questions.passage:
Text 1

Many educators believe that homework builds discipline and reinforces classroom learning, and they point to studies showing a modest correlation between time spent on homework and grades among high school students.

Text 2

Psychologist Dana Cole notes that the correlation between homework and grades weakens or disappears among younger students. She argues that for elementary students, time spent on homework would be better spent on reading for pleasure and on unstructured play.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would Cole (Text 2) most likely respond to the educators described in Text 1?
choices: By arguing that homework should be eliminated at every grade level.
By noting that the benefits they cite may not apply to younger students.
By agreeing that homework improves grades for students of all ages.
By questioning whether discipline can be measured at all.
questions.explanation: Cole does not dispute the high school correlation; she points out it fades for younger students, which is B. A goes further than she does (she addresses elementary students only), C contradicts her, and D raises a point neither text makes.

questions.passage: The museum's new wing was designed to maximize natural light. ______ nearly every gallery has floor-to-ceiling windows.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The second sentence is a consequence of the design goal in the first, so a cause-and-effect transition fits: "Accordingly." The other three all signal contrast, which the sentences do not have.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• The Great Green Wall is a project to plant a belt of trees and restore land across Africa's Sahel region.
• It was launched in 2007 by the African Union.
• Its goal is to restore 100 million hectares of degraded land by 2030.
• As of 2023, roughly 18 million hectares had been restored.
• The project also aims to create millions of jobs.
questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize how much of the project's land-restoration goal remains unmet. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Launched in 2007, the Great Green Wall aims to restore land across Africa's Sahel region.
By 2023, the Great Green Wall had restored about 18 million hectares, less than a fifth of its 100-million-hectare goal.
The Great Green Wall is expected to create millions of jobs in the Sahel.
The African Union launched the Great Green Wall to restore 100 million hectares by 2030.
questions.explanation: Only B puts the progress (18 million) next to the goal (100 million) and states the gap, which is exactly what the student wants to emphasize. A, C, and D each state a fact from the notes but say nothing about how much remains.

questions.passage: The collection of essays, which spans three decades of the author's career, ______ readers a rare view of her evolving style.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular noun "collection" (not "essays," which sits inside the prepositional phrase "of essays"), so the verb must be singular: "offers."

questions.passage: Three elements make the bridge remarkable: its ______ its span, and its age.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The blank sits between the first and second items of a simple three-item list, which are separated by commas. Semicolons separate list items only when the items themselves contain commas; a colon or dash would wrongly break the list.

questions.passage: Originally scheduled for March, ______
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: the launch was pushed back to May by the engineering team.
the engineering team pushed the launch back to May.
May became the new date chosen by the engineering team.
the engineering team's plans for the launch were pushed back to May.
questions.explanation: The opening modifier "Originally scheduled for March" must describe the noun that follows it. Only the launch was scheduled for March, so "the launch" has to come right after the comma. B makes the team the scheduled thing, C makes May, and D makes the team's plans.

questions.passage: Although the novel was praised for its ambitious scope, some critics found its plot ______, noting that several storylines were introduced and then abandoned.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Storylines that are introduced and then abandoned make a plot broken into pieces: "fragmented." "Cohesive" is the opposite, and neither "conventional" nor "restrained" describes abandoned storylines.

questions.stem: If 3x + 7 = 22, what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Subtract 7 from both sides: 3x = 15. Divide by 3: x = 5.

questions.stem: A gym charges a one-time membership fee of $40 plus $25 per month. Which equation gives the total cost C, in dollars, of a membership lasting m months?
questions.explanation: The $40 is paid once, so it is the constant term. The $25 repeats each month, so it multiplies m: C = 40 + 25m. Choice A swaps the two amounts.

questions.stem:
The system of equations below has no solution. What is the value of k?

2x + 3y = 12
4x + ky = 20
questions.explanation: A system has no solution when the lines are parallel: same slope, different intercepts. Multiplying the first equation by 2 gives 4x + 6y = 24. For the second line to be parallel, its y-coefficient must match: k = 6. The constants differ (24 vs. 20), so the lines are distinct and never meet.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to (x + 3)(x − 5)?
questions.explanation: Expand: x·x = x², x·(−5) = −5x, 3·x = 3x, 3·(−5) = −15. Combine the middle terms: −5x + 3x = −2x. Result: x² − 2x − 15.

questions.stem: The population of a town is 8,000 and increases by 5% each year. Which function models the population P(t) after t years?
questions.explanation: A 5% yearly increase multiplies the population by 1.05 each year, so after t years it is 8000 × 1.05ᵗ. Choice B multiplies by 0.05 (a 95% drop), C is linear rather than exponential, and D uses 50% growth.

questions.stem: The equation x² − 6x + c = 0 has exactly one real solution. What is the value of c?
questions.explanation: A quadratic has exactly one real solution when its discriminant is zero: b² − 4ac = 0. Here (−6)² − 4(1)(c) = 36 − 4c = 0, so c = 9. (Check: x² − 6x + 9 = (x − 3)², one solution at x = 3.)

questions.stem: A jacket originally priced at $80 is on sale for 25% off. What is the sale price of the jacket?
questions.explanation: 25% of $80 is $20, so the discount is $20 and the sale price is $80 − $20 = $60. Choice A is the discount itself, not the price.

questions.skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
questions.stem: A car travels 210 miles using 6 gallons of gasoline. At the same rate, how many gallons of gasoline are needed to travel 350 miles?
questions.explanation: The rate is 210 ÷ 6 = 35 miles per gallon. For 350 miles: 350 ÷ 35 = 10 gallons. Equivalently, set up the proportion 210/6 = 350/g and solve for g.

questions.skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
questions.stem: The mean of a list of five numbers is 12. When a sixth number is added to the list, the mean of the six numbers is 14. What is the sixth number?
questions.explanation: Mean × count = total. Five numbers with mean 12 total 5 × 12 = 60. Six numbers with mean 14 total 6 × 14 = 84. The sixth number is the difference: 84 − 60 = 24.

questions.stem: A rectangle has a length of 12 centimeters and a width of 5 centimeters. What is the area of the rectangle, in square centimeters?
questions.explanation: Area of a rectangle = length × width = 12 × 5 = 60. Choice A is the sum of the sides and B is the perimeter.

questions.stem: A right triangle has legs of length 9 and 12. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
questions.explanation: By the Pythagorean theorem, hypotenuse² = 9² + 12² = 81 + 144 = 225, so the hypotenuse is √225 = 15. (This is the 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 3.)

questions.stem: A circle in the xy-plane has the equation x² + y² − 6x + 4y = 12. What is the radius of the circle?
questions.explanation: Complete the square for each variable. x² − 6x becomes (x − 3)² − 9, and y² + 4y becomes (y + 2)² − 4. So (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² − 13 = 12, giving (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25. The radius is √25 = 5; choice D is the radius squared.

questions.passage: In a 2019 survey of 40 city blocks, researchers found that blocks with mature street trees had summer surface temperatures up to 6°C lower than blocks without them. The effect was strongest where tree canopy covered at least 40 percent of the sidewalk. The researchers caution, however, that newly planted saplings provide little cooling during their first decade.
questions.stem: According to the text, what did the researchers find about newly planted saplings?
choices: They lower surface temperatures as effectively as mature trees do.
They provide little cooling for roughly their first ten years.
They survive best on blocks with at least 40 percent canopy cover.
They raise surface temperatures on the blocks where they are planted.
questions.explanation: The last sentence states directly that saplings "provide little cooling during their first decade," which is choice B. A contradicts that sentence, C connects two details the text never links, and D is not stated anywhere.

questions.passage:
Tutoring hours by volunteer, fall semester

Volunteer   Sept   Oct   Nov
Ana          12     15    18
Ben          20     14     9
Chloe         8      8     8
Dev           5     11    17

A student reviewing the table claims that one volunteer's tutoring hours declined every month.
questions.stem: Which choice best supports the student's claim?
choices: Ana tutored 12 hours in September and 18 hours in November.
Ben tutored 20 hours in September, 14 in October, and 9 in November.
Chloe tutored 8 hours in each of the three months.
Dev tutored more hours in November than in September.
questions.explanation: The claim needs a volunteer whose hours drop from each month to the next. Only Ben's do: 20, then 14, then 9. Ana and Dev increase, and Chloe stays flat.

questions.passage: Coral reefs depend on a partnership with tiny algae that live inside the coral and supply it with most of its food. When ocean water becomes too warm, corals expel the algae and turn white, a process called bleaching. Bleached corals are not dead, but because they have lost their main food source, ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: they recover fully as soon as the water temperature changes.
they can starve if the water does not cool soon enough for the algae to return.
they begin producing their own food instead.
they no longer depend on the surrounding water.
questions.explanation: The setup is that the algae supply most of the coral's food and bleaching means losing them. The logical consequence is that a bleached coral risks starving unless the algae come back, which is B. A ignores the food problem, and C and D contradict the dependence the text establishes.

questions.passage: Most people picture a desert as endless sand. In fact, only about a quarter of the Sahara is sand dunes; the rest is gravel plains, rocky plateaus, and salt flats.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It presents a common assumption and then corrects it.
It describes a problem and then proposes a solution.
It lists several deserts in order of size.
It explains the process by which deserts form.
questions.explanation: "Most people picture..." sets up the assumption; "In fact..." corrects it with the real makeup of the Sahara. No problem or solution is raised, no other deserts are named, and formation is never discussed.

questions.passage:
Text 1

Scholars have long attributed the anonymous fourteenth-century poem to a single author, pointing to its consistent style and unified structure.

Text 2

Linguist Mara Feld analyzed the poem's vocabulary and found two distinct dialect patterns concentrated in different sections. She argues that this distribution is difficult to explain if only one person wrote the poem.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would Feld (Text 2) most likely respond to the scholars described in Text 1?
choices: By agreeing that the poem's unified structure proves a single author wrote it.
By suggesting that consistency of style does not rule out more than one author.
By arguing that the poem was written after the fourteenth century.
By claiming that the poem has no unified structure at all.
questions.explanation: Feld's evidence (two dialect patterns) points toward multiple authors even though the style is consistent, so she would say consistency alone does not settle the question: B. She does not dispute the structure (D) or the date (C), and A is the opposite of her position.

questions.passage: Solar panels have become far cheaper over the past decade. ______ many homeowners still hesitate to install them because of the upfront cost.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The second sentence runs against what the first would lead you to expect (cheaper panels, yet hesitation), so a concessive transition is needed: "Even so." "As a result" would claim the hesitation follows from the price drop, and the other two do not signal contrast.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Wangari Maathai was a Kenyan environmental activist.
• In 1977 she founded the Green Belt Movement.
• The movement paid rural women to plant trees.
• By 2004 the movement had planted more than 30 million trees.
• In 2004 Maathai became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
questions.stem: The student wants to convey the scale of the Green Belt Movement to an audience unfamiliar with Maathai. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Wangari Maathai won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004.
Kenyan activist Wangari Maathai's Green Belt Movement, founded in 1977, had planted more than 30 million trees by 2004.
The Green Belt Movement paid rural women to plant trees.
Maathai, the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize, founded a movement.
questions.explanation: The audience needs to be told who Maathai is (Kenyan activist) and given the scale (30 million trees). Only B does both. A and D are about the prize, not the movement's scale, and C describes the method without any numbers.

questions.passage: The observatory's telescope, which was installed in ______ remains one of the largest of its kind.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: "which was installed in 1962" is a nonessential clause opened by a comma after "telescope," so it must be closed by a matching comma. A semicolon or colon would break the sentence, and leaving the clause unclosed is also wrong.

questions.passage: The kit includes everything a beginner ______ a board, a set of pieces, and an instruction booklet.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: What follows the blank is a list that explains "everything a beginner needs," and it is not an independent clause. A colon introduces such a list. A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and a comma or nothing would run the list into the sentence.

questions.passage: By the time the rescue team arrived, the hikers ______ two nights on the ridge.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: "By the time the rescue team arrived" places one past event before another past event, which calls for the past perfect: "had spent." The other tenses do not sit before a past arrival.

questions.stem: The line y = 2x − 3 passes through the point (4, k). What is the value of k?
questions.explanation: Substitute x = 4: y = 2(4) − 3 = 8 − 3 = 5. So k = 5.

questions.stem: Which of the following values of x satisfies the inequality 4x − 5 > 11?
questions.explanation: Add 5 to both sides: 4x > 16. Divide by 4: x > 4. The only choice greater than 4 is 5. Note that 4 itself does not work, since the inequality is strict.

questions.stem: A scatterplot shows the relationship between the number of hours per day a plant is exposed to sunlight, s, and its height, h, in centimeters. The line of best fit is h = 3.2s + 4. According to the model, what is the predicted increase in height for each additional hour of daily sunlight?
questions.explanation: In h = 3.2s + 4, the slope 3.2 is the change in h for each 1-unit increase in s. The 4 is the predicted height with zero sunlight (the intercept), not a rate.

questions.stem: A bag contains 5 red marbles, 3 blue marbles, and 2 green marbles. If one marble is selected at random, what is the probability that it is not red?
questions.explanation: There are 10 marbles in all and 5 are not red (3 blue + 2 green), so the probability is 5/10 = 1/2. Equivalently, 1 − P(red) = 1 − 5/10.

questions.stem: Two angles of a triangle measure 35° and 65°. What is the measure, in degrees, of the third angle?
questions.explanation: The angles of a triangle sum to 180°: 180 − 35 − 65 = 80.

questions.skill: Systems of equations in two variables
questions.stem: The graphs of y = x² and y = 2x + 3 intersect at two points. What is the sum of the x-coordinates of those points?
questions.explanation: Set the equations equal: x² = 2x + 3, so x² − 2x − 3 = 0, which factors as (x − 3)(x + 1) = 0. The x-coordinates are 3 and −1, and their sum is 2. (Shortcut: for x² + bx + c = 0 the roots sum to −b, here 2.)

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.stem: A random sample of 400 students at a school with 2,000 students found that 30% of the sample walk to school. Based on the sample, which of the following is the best estimate of the number of students at the school who walk to school?
questions.explanation: A random sample lets you apply its proportion to the whole population: 30% of 2,000 = 600. Choice A applies 30% to the sample instead of the school.

questions.skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
questions.stem: A recipe uses 3 cups of flour for every 2 cups of sugar. How many cups of flour are needed for 8 cups of sugar?
questions.explanation: Set up the proportion 3/2 = f/8. Cross-multiply: 2f = 24, so f = 12. Or notice 8 cups of sugar is 4 times the recipe, so 4 × 3 = 12 cups of flour.

questions.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = x² − 4x + 7. What is the minimum value of f(x)?
questions.explanation: The parabola opens upward, so its minimum is at the vertex, x = −b/(2a) = 4/2 = 2. Then f(2) = 4 − 8 + 7 = 3. Choice B is the x-coordinate of the vertex, not the minimum value.

questions.stem: The price of an item is increased by 20%, and then the new price is decreased by 20%. The final price is what percent of the original price?
questions.explanation: Multiply the factors: 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96, so the final price is 96% of the original. The percentages do not cancel because the 20% decrease is taken from a larger number than the 20% increase was added to.

questions.stem: A right circular cylinder has a radius of 3 and a height of 10. What is the volume of the cylinder?
questions.explanation: Volume of a cylinder = πr²h = π(3²)(10) = π(9)(10) = 90π.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to determine whether a new fertilizer causes tomato plants to grow taller. Which study design best supports a cause-and-effect conclusion?
choices: Survey gardeners who chose to use the fertilizer about their plants' heights.
Randomly assign tomato plants to receive either the fertilizer or no fertilizer, then compare the heights.
Measure the tallest plants in a garden that uses the fertilizer.
Compare plant heights in two gardens that already differ in whether they use the fertilizer.
questions.explanation: Only random assignment to treatment and control groups supports a cause-and-effect conclusion, because it spreads other differences evenly between the groups. The other designs are observational: the gardens or gardeners chose the fertilizer themselves, so anything else about them could explain a height difference.

questions.passage: Honeybees communicate the location of food through a "waggle dance." A returning forager moves in a figure-eight pattern; the angle of the dance's central run relative to vertical indicates the direction of the food relative to the sun, and the duration of the run indicates the distance.
questions.stem: According to the text, what does the duration of the waggle run communicate to other bees?
questions.explanation: The text pairs each feature of the dance with what it encodes: the angle gives direction, and "the duration of the run indicates the distance." Quality and forager numbers are never mentioned, and the sun's position is the reference point for direction, not what duration conveys.

questions.passage: In 1854 the physician John Snow mapped cholera deaths in London and noticed that they clustered around a single public water pump on Broad Street. When the pump's handle was removed, new cases in the area fell sharply. Snow's map is often cited as an early example of using data visualization to investigate the cause of a disease.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Cholera was eliminated from London in 1854.
Snow used a map of deaths to trace an outbreak to a water source.
Public water pumps were a common cause of disease in the nineteenth century.
Data visualization was invented by John Snow.
questions.explanation: Every sentence serves the story of Snow tracing the outbreak to the pump with his map, which is B. A overstates the outcome (cases fell in one area), C generalizes beyond one pump, and D is not claimed; the text says his map is an "early example," not the first.

questions.passage: Although the octopus has a large central brain, roughly two thirds of its neurons are located in its arms. Each arm can process sensory information and coordinate its own movement with little direction from the brain. Researchers have even observed a severed arm continuing to grasp objects for some time, which suggests that the arms possess a degree of independent control.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Octopus arms operate with considerable independence from the central brain.
The octopus has more neurons than any other invertebrate.
A severed octopus arm can regrow within weeks.
The central brain of an octopus is unusually small.
questions.explanation: The neuron count, the arms' own processing, and the severed-arm observation all build to one point: the arms act with independence, choice A. B makes a comparison the text never makes, C describes regrowth, which is not mentioned, and D contradicts the opening, which calls the brain large.

questions.passage: The town library's circulation numbers tell a more complicated story than the headline decline suggests. Checkouts of printed books have fallen by 18 percent over five years, but downloads of e-books and audiobooks have more than tripled in the same period, so the total number of items borrowed has actually risen.
questions.stem: According to the text, which of the following is true of the total number of items borrowed from the library over the five-year period?
questions.explanation: The last clause states it directly: the total "has actually risen." A is the figure for printed books only, B is the figure for digital downloads only, and D is contradicted by the text.

questions.passage: Historians once treated the medieval "Little Ice Age" as a uniform cooling that gripped the entire Northern Hemisphere from the fourteenth to the nineteenth century. Tree-ring and ice-core records now show a patchier picture: sharp cold decades in some regions coincided with mild ones elsewhere, and the timing of the coldest intervals differed from continent to continent. The label survives, but it describes a tendency rather than a single event.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The Little Ice Age never actually occurred.
Newer evidence shows that the Little Ice Age was far less uniform than the traditional account suggested.
Tree-ring records are more reliable than ice-core records.
The Little Ice Age was coldest during the fourteenth century.
questions.explanation: The text moves from the old view (uniform cooling) to what newer records show (patchy, regionally varied), then concludes the label now names a tendency, not an event. That is B. A goes too far: the label "survives." C ranks two sources the text treats together, and D is a detail the text never gives.

questions.passage: Poet Lucille Clifton wrote in short, unpunctuated lines that reviewers sometimes dismissed as simple. Her defenders argue that the plainness is the achievement: by stripping away ornament, Clifton makes each word carry weight, so that a poem of thirty words can hold as much as a page of dense verse.
questions.stem: According to the text, how do Clifton's defenders respond to the charge that her poetry is simple?
choices: They deny that her lines are unusually short.
They argue that the simplicity is deliberate and gives each word greater weight.
They point out that she used more punctuation in her later work.
They claim that the reviewers did not read her poems carefully.
questions.explanation: The defenders accept the plainness and reframe it as the point: stripping ornament makes each word "carry weight." That is B. They do not dispute the description of her lines (A), nothing is said about later work (C), or about how carefully reviewers read (D).

questions.passage: Before mechanical refrigeration, ice was harvested from frozen lakes in winter, packed in sawdust, and shipped as far as India. In the 1830s the Boston merchant Frederic Tudor built a business on this trade, and for a time ice was one of New England's leading exports.
questions.stem: According to the text, how was harvested ice kept from melting during shipment?
choices: It was shipped only during the winter months.
It was stored in underground cellars.
It was kept in refrigerated holds.
questions.explanation: The text says the ice was "packed in sawdust" for shipping. Winter is when it was harvested, not when it was shipped (A); cellars are not mentioned (C); and refrigeration is what the text says did not yet exist (D).

questions.passage: Contrary to the popular image of a lone inventor, the electric light bulb was refined by dozens of people over several decades. Thomas Edison's contribution was less the idea of an electric lamp than a durable filament and, crucially, a system of generators and wiring that made the lamp practical for ordinary homes.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Edison did not contribute anything original to the light bulb.
Edison's key contribution was making the electric lamp practical rather than conceiving the idea of it.
The light bulb was perfected within a single decade.
Generators are more important than lamps.
questions.explanation: The text pushes against the lone-inventor image and then locates Edison's real contribution in the filament and the supporting system, which is B. A overshoots (the filament and system were contributions), C contradicts "several decades," and D turns a supporting detail into a ranking the text never makes.

questions.passage: A survey of 1,200 commuters found that those who biked to work reported higher satisfaction with their commute than those who drove, even when the bike trip took longer. The researchers noted that cyclists described their commute as time they controlled, whereas drivers described theirs as time lost to traffic.
questions.stem: According to the text, how did cyclists describe their commute?
questions.explanation: The last sentence quotes the contrast: cyclists called their commute "time they controlled." D is what drivers said, A is contradicted (the bike trip often took longer), and safety is never mentioned.

questions.passage: The idea that we use only ten percent of our brains has no basis in neuroscience. Imaging studies show activity throughout the brain over the course of a day, and damage to almost any region produces some measurable deficit. The myth probably persists because it flatters us: it implies vast untapped potential rather than the more modest truth that the whole organ is already working.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The ten-percent claim is false, and it endures because it is more flattering than the truth.
People should try to use more of their brains.
Damage to the brain rarely causes lasting deficits.
questions.explanation: The first two sentences establish that the claim is false; the third explains why it survives anyway. B captures both halves. A and D contradict the evidence the text cites, and C accepts the myth the text is debunking.

questions.passage: Lichens are not single organisms but partnerships: a fungus provides structure and holds water, while an alga or cyanobacterium living inside it produces food through photosynthesis. Together they can grow on bare rock where neither partner could survive alone.
questions.stem: According to the text, what does the fungus contribute to the lichen partnership?
questions.explanation: The text assigns roles explicitly: the fungus "provides structure and holds water," and the alga does the photosynthesis. Reproduction and color are not discussed.

questions.passage: When the city replaced a four-lane road with two lanes and a bike path, planners expected serious delays. Instead, average travel times on the road barely changed, because a share of drivers switched to other routes or to cycling. The finding echoes studies elsewhere showing that road capacity shapes demand rather than simply serving it.
questions.stem: According to the text, why did travel times barely change after the road was narrowed?
choices: The city installed additional traffic signals.
Some drivers changed routes or began cycling.
The road was later widened again.
Fewer people lived in the city than planners assumed.
questions.explanation: The text gives the reason directly: "a share of drivers switched to other routes or to cycling." None of the other explanations appears in the text.

questions.passage: Biologist Lena Ortiz claims that street noise causes urban songbirds to sing at higher pitches than their rural counterparts do.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ortiz's claim?
choices: Urban birds sing at higher pitches than rural birds, and their pitch rises further on days when traffic noise is heavier.
Urban birds are, on average, larger than rural birds of the same species.
Rural birds begin singing earlier in the morning than urban birds.
Urban birds sing more often than rural birds do.
questions.explanation: The claim links noise to pitch. Choice A shows both the urban-rural pitch difference and pitch tracking noise levels, which points to noise as the cause. B, C, and D describe differences in size, timing, and frequency of song, none of which bear on pitch.

questions.passage: A student argues that a school's new later start time improved students' attendance.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the student's argument?
choices: Students reported that they liked the later start time.
In the year after the change, average daily attendance rose from 91 percent to 95 percent, while attendance at nearby schools that kept their old schedules stayed flat.
Teachers reported that students seemed more alert in first period.
The school's average test scores rose the following year.
questions.explanation: Only B measures attendance itself, and the comparison with unchanged nearby schools rules out a district-wide trend as the explanation. A and C are opinions about alertness or preference, and D is about test scores, not attendance.

questions.passage:
Average reaction time by hours of sleep, in a study of 80 adults

Hours of sleep   Reaction time (ms)
4                  312
6                  271
8                  244
10                 246

A researcher claims that beyond a certain amount, additional sleep produces no further improvement in reaction time.
questions.stem: Which choice best uses data from the table to support the researcher's claim?
choices: Participants who slept 4 hours had the slowest reaction times.
Reaction time improved from 4 to 6 hours of sleep and again from 6 to 8 hours.
Reaction times at 8 and 10 hours were nearly identical, even though the second group slept two hours longer.
The study measured 80 adults at four different amounts of sleep.
questions.explanation: The claim is about a point past which more sleep stops helping. Only C identifies that point: 8 to 10 hours brought no improvement (244 vs. 246 ms). A and B describe the range where sleep does help, and D is about the study's design.

questions.passage: Archaeologist Tomas Reyes hypothesizes that the inhabitants of an ancient coastal settlement traded with communities far inland.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Reyes's hypothesis?
choices: The settlement's pottery was made from clay found nearby.
Excavations at the settlement uncovered obsidian tools whose chemical signature matches a quarry 300 miles inland.
The settlement was abandoned around 900 CE.
Fish bones make up most of the food remains at the site.
questions.explanation: Obsidian from a quarry 300 miles inland could only have reached the coast through contact with inland communities, which is exactly what the hypothesis proposes. A points to local production, and C and D say nothing about contact with the interior.

questions.passage: A gardener claims that spreading mulch around tomato plants reduces how often they need to be watered.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the gardener's claim?
choices: Mulched plots retained soil moisture twice as long as unmulched plots after the same amount of watering.
Mulched plots produced larger tomatoes than unmulched plots.
Tomato plants grow best in full sun.
questions.explanation: The claim is about watering frequency, which depends on how long soil stays moist. A measures exactly that. B is about fruit size, and C and D do not involve mulch's effect on water at all.

questions.passage: Literary critic Ada Wren argues that the narrator of a certain novel is unreliable and that the author signals this unreliability deliberately.
questions.stem: Which quotation from the novel would most directly support Wren's argument?
choices: "I have always told the truth, whatever others may say of me."
"The house had seven windows; or was it six? I counted them twice and got a different answer each time."
"The rain fell steadily through the afternoon and into the night."
"My sister arrived on the evening train, as she had promised."
questions.explanation: An unreliable narrator is one whose account cannot be trusted. B shows the narrator unable to report a simple fact consistently, a clear authorial signal. A is a narrator's claim of honesty, which by itself neither proves nor disproves reliability, and C and D are plain statements with nothing to doubt.

questions.passage:
Number of bird species recorded in a park, by year

Year   Species
2019    48
2020    51
2021    47
2022    63
2023    66

A park ranger claims that the wetland restored in early 2022 attracted new bird species to the park.
questions.stem: Which choice best uses data from the table to support the ranger's claim?
choices: The number of species rose from 48 in 2019 to 51 in 2020.
The number of species dipped slightly in 2021.
The count jumped from 47 in 2021 to 63 in 2022, the year the wetland was restored, and stayed high in 2023.
The park recorded species in five consecutive years.
questions.explanation: The claim ties new species to the 2022 restoration, so the supporting data must show a change at 2022. C does: a 16-species jump that year, sustained the next. A and B describe the years before the restoration, and D is about the record-keeping.

questions.passage: An economist claims that a city's rent-control policy reduced the number of apartments available to rent.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the economist's claim?
choices: Rents in the city rose in the years after the policy took effect.
In the five years after the policy took effect, the number of units offered for rent fell by 12 percent as owners converted apartments into condominiums for sale.
Tenants in rent-controlled units reported high satisfaction with their housing.
Several other cities adopted similar policies.
questions.explanation: The claim is about the supply of rental units. Only B measures that supply and shows it falling after the policy, with a mechanism (conversion to condominiums). A is about prices, C about satisfaction, and D about other cities.

questions.passage: Musicologist Priya Nair argues that the composer revised the symphony's final movement after its premiere in response to critical reviews.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Nair's argument?
choices: The manuscript of the final movement shows changes in an ink that matches letters the composer wrote the month after the premiere, and those letters discuss the reviews.
The symphony was performed many times in the years after the premiere.
The composer wrote several other symphonies later in life.
questions.explanation: Nair's argument has two parts: the revision happened after the premiere, and it was a response to critics. B supports both, dating the changes by ink to the weeks after the premiere and connecting them to letters about the reviews. A cuts against the argument, and C and D are unrelated.

questions.passage: A coach believes that a new warm-up routine reduces the number of injuries on the team.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the coach's belief?
choices: Injuries fell from 14 to 5 in the season after the routine was introduced, with the same players and the same schedule.
Players said they enjoyed the new routine.
The team won more games after adopting the routine.
The routine takes about ten minutes to complete.
questions.explanation: Only A measures injuries and compares before and after while holding players and schedule constant. B is about enjoyment, C about wins, and D about duration.

questions.passage: A researcher claims that a certain species of moth uses the moon to keep a straight course when it flies at night.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researcher's claim?
choices: The moths flew in consistent straight lines on clear moonlit nights but circled aimlessly when the moon was hidden by cloud.
The moths are strongly attracted to porch lights.
The moths fly mostly between dusk and midnight.
Moth populations are largest in late summer.
questions.explanation: If the moon is the cue, flight should be straight when the moon is visible and disordered when it is not. A shows exactly that contrast. B, C, and D say nothing about how the moths hold a course.

questions.passage:
Share of households with home internet access, by region

Region    2015    2023
North     72%     94%
South     58%     91%
East      80%     95%
West      65%     89%

A journalist claims that the gap in internet access between regions narrowed sharply between 2015 and 2023.
questions.stem: Which choice best uses data from the table to support the journalist's claim?
choices: The North had 72 percent access in 2015.
Every region exceeded 89 percent access by 2023.
In 2015, access ranged from 58 to 80 percent, a 22-point spread; by 2023 it ranged from 89 to 95 percent, a 6-point spread.
The East had the highest access in both years.
questions.explanation: The claim is about the gap between regions, so the evidence must compare the spread in each year. C does: 22 points in 2015 down to 6 in 2023. A is a single value, B shows every region is high but not that they are close together, and D is about rank order, not the gap.

questions.passage: Desert plants lose precious water through their leaves, so many species have evolved tiny leaves or none at all. The saguaro cactus, for instance, ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: has broad leaves to capture as much sunlight as possible.
carries out photosynthesis in its thick green stem rather than in leaves.
grows only in regions with reliable rainfall.
sheds its stem each summer to conserve water.
questions.explanation: The text says desert plants avoid water loss by having few or no leaves, and the saguaro is introduced as an example. The completion must show it doing without leaves, which is B. A gives it broad leaves, C removes it from the desert, and D describes something no plant does.

questions.passage: Studies of chess experts find that they recall the positions of pieces from real games far better than novices do. But when pieces are placed randomly on the board, the experts' recall drops to nearly the novice level. This suggests that the experts' advantage comes not from superior memory in general but from ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: years of playing against stronger opponents.
their ability to recognize familiar patterns of play.
the speed with which they can move the pieces.
a talent for memorizing random information.
questions.explanation: Experts excel only with positions that could occur in real games, so their edge must come from recognizing meaningful patterns, not raw memory: B. D is contradicted by the random-position result, and A and C are never mentioned.

questions.passage: Some species of ants farm fungus, feeding it plant material and eating the fungus in turn. The fungus cannot survive outside the ants' nests, and the ants cannot digest most plant material directly. A biologist studying the relationship would therefore be justified in concluding that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the ants could easily switch to a different food source.
each partner depends on the other for its survival.
the fungus is a parasite that harms the ants.
the ants acquired the fungus only recently.
questions.explanation: The text gives one constraint for each partner: the fungus needs the nest, and the ants need the fungus to make plants edible. Together those mean mutual dependence, B. A contradicts the ants' digestive limit, C contradicts the benefit the ants receive, and D concerns history the text does not address.

questions.passage: Roman concrete has endured for two thousand years in seawater that destroys modern concrete within decades. Chemical analysis shows that the Roman mixture contained volcanic ash, which reacts with seawater to form crystals that fill cracks as they appear. This finding suggests that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: modern concrete is stronger than Roman concrete when first poured.
Roman builders understood the chemistry of their materials as well as modern engineers do.
the durability of Roman concrete owes something to an ingredient that lets it repair itself.
seawater strengthens every kind of concrete over time.
questions.explanation: Crystals that fill cracks as they form are a self-repair mechanism, and the text links that to the volcanic ash: C. A is about initial strength, which is not discussed; B claims knowledge the text does not attribute to the Romans; D contradicts the opening sentence about modern concrete.

questions.passage: Because sound travels farther through water than through air, whales can communicate over enormous distances; a call from one whale may reach another hundreds of miles away. Ship traffic, however, fills the ocean with low-frequency noise, so ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: whales have stopped communicating with one another.
whale calls may be drowned out before they reach distant listeners.
whales now communicate mainly through the air.
ships have become quieter in response.
questions.explanation: "However" sets up a problem for long-distance calls, and noise in the same frequency range would interfere with them: B. A and C go far beyond what the text supports, and D reverses the direction of the problem.

questions.passage: In the eighteenth century most European cities had no house numbers; letters were addressed by landmarks and descriptions. Numbering was introduced mainly so that governments could locate residents for taxation and conscription, and it was often resisted for precisely that reason. This history suggests that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: house numbers were adopted because residents demanded them.
a convenience now taken for granted began as an instrument of state control.
letters could not be delivered before numbering existed.
taxation was rare before the eighteenth century.
questions.explanation: Numbering was imposed for the state's purposes and resisted by residents, so the modern convenience has its origin in control: B. A contradicts the resistance, C contradicts the first sentence (letters were addressed by description), and D is not supported.

questions.passage: A study tracked two groups of students learning a language. One group practiced for fifteen minutes every day; the other practiced once a week for two hours. After three months the daily group scored significantly higher on vocabulary tests, even though the two groups' total study time was roughly equal. The results suggest that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: longer study sessions are always more effective than shorter ones.
how study time is distributed matters, not only how much of it there is.
vocabulary cannot be learned in weekly sessions.
the weekly group studied less overall than the daily group.
questions.explanation: Total time was equal and only the distribution differed, so the difference in scores must come from distribution: B. A is the reverse of the finding, C overstates it (the weekly group learned, just less), and D is ruled out by the text.

questions.passage: A restaurant found that after it began printing calorie counts on its menu, orders of its highest-calorie dishes fell by a quarter. Since the dishes, their prices, and their portions were otherwise unchanged, the drop most likely resulted from ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: a change in the restaurant's location.
customers using the new information when deciding what to order.
questions.explanation: The text rules out changes to dishes, prices, and portions, leaving the new calorie information as the only thing that changed: B. C and D are explicitly excluded, and A is not mentioned.

questions.passage: Fossils of feathered dinosaurs have been found in rocks far older than the earliest known bird. Many of these animals were flightless, and some of their feathers were simple filaments unsuited to flight. Paleontologists therefore infer that feathers ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: evolved specifically to make flight possible.
first served some purpose other than flight, such as insulation or display.
appeared only after birds had evolved.
questions.explanation: Feathers that predate birds, on animals that could not fly, with structures unsuited to flight, cannot have arisen for flight; they must have done something else first: B. A and C are contradicted by the fossils' age and the flightless animals, and D is not supported.

questions.passage: The town's only bridge closed for repairs for six weeks. Shopkeepers on the far side of the river braced for a collapse in business, but sales fell only slightly, and several reported new customers who lived nearby and had previously driven across the bridge to shop elsewhere. This suggests that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the bridge closure was extended beyond six weeks.
some nearby residents changed their shopping habits during the closure.
most of the shops' customers came from across the river.
the shops raised their prices to make up for lost sales.
questions.explanation: The new customers were locals who used to cross the bridge to shop elsewhere; with the bridge closed, they shopped nearby instead: B. C is undercut by the small drop in sales, and A and D are not mentioned.

questions.passage: Tree rings are wider in years with ample rain and narrower in dry years. Timbers from a medieval barn show a run of five very narrow rings ending around 1315, the year in which chronicles first record a great famine. A historian could reasonably infer that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the barn was built long after the famine ended.
the famine was preceded by several years of drought.
tree rings are an unreliable guide to past weather.
the chroniclers exaggerated the severity of the famine.
questions.explanation: Five narrow rings mean five dry years, and they end in the famine's first year, so drought came just before the famine: B. A, C, and D are not supported by anything in the text.

questions.passage: Economists have long assumed that people spend windfall money, such as a tax refund, the same way they spend any other income. Yet surveys find that people treat refunds as "found money" and are far more likely to spend them on treats than they would an equivalent raise in salary. This pattern implies that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: tax refunds are usually larger than salary raises.
people's spending decisions depend partly on how they mentally label money, not only on the amount.
people never save money that comes as a windfall.
salary raises are usually spent on treats.
questions.explanation: The same amount of money is spent differently depending on whether it is labeled a refund or a raise, so the label matters: B. A is about size, which the text holds equal; C and D overstate what the surveys show.

questions.passage: The old map was so ______ that the coastline it showed bore little resemblance to the actual shore.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: A coastline that does not resemble the real shore makes the map inaccurate. "Accurate" is the opposite, and colorful or valuable say nothing about how the map matches reality.

questions.passage: The volunteers were ______ in their support, arriving early and staying late every weekend.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Arriving early and staying late every weekend shows effort that never flags: tireless. Reluctant and occasional describe the opposite, and silent is unrelated.

questions.passage: The negotiator's tone was deliberately ______: she neither promised nor refused anything, leaving both sides room to maneuver.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Neither promising nor refusing is the definition of noncommittal. Hostile and enthusiastic would each commit her to a side, and precise is the opposite of leaving room to maneuver.

questions.passage: Early critics found the painter's colors ______, but later generations came to see the clashing tones as bold rather than careless.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The colors are described as clashing, and the critics' view was negative, so they found them garish. Harmonious is the opposite of clashing, and subdued or faded colors would not clash.

questions.passage: The senator's answer was a model of ______: it ran for five minutes without committing her to a single position.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: A long answer that commits to nothing is evasive. Candor and precision would mean saying something definite, and brevity is ruled out by the five minutes.

questions.passage: Although the two species look nearly identical, their songs are ______, and experienced birders learn to tell them apart by ear.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: "Although" contrasts identical looks with the songs, and birders can tell the birds apart by ear, so the songs must be distinctive. "Indistinguishable" would make that impossible, and faint or melodious does not set up the contrast.

questions.passage: The historian is careful to ______ between what the documents prove and what they merely suggest.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: To separate proof from suggestion is to distinguish between them. Alternate and waver imply switching back and forth, and mediate means to settle a dispute.

questions.passage: The trail is well ______, with signs at every junction, so hikers rarely lose their way.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Signs at every junction make a trail well marked. Hidden would cause hikers to get lost, and worn or crowded do not explain why they don't.

questions.passage: Rather than ______ the criticism, the director invited the reviewer to the next rehearsal.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: "Rather than" contrasts the director's open response with the opposite reaction, which would be to dismiss the criticism. Welcoming is not a contrast with inviting the reviewer, and repeating or analyzing do not fit the sentence's logic.

questions.passage: The essay's argument is ______: each claim rests on evidence, and each section builds on the one before.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Claims supported by evidence and sections that build in order describe a rigorous argument. Tentative means uncertain, meandering means unfocused, and ornate describes decoration, not logic.

questions.passage: The drought left the reservoir so ______ that the tops of drowned trees, unseen for decades, broke the surface.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Trees hidden underwater for decades reappearing means the water level dropped far: depleted. Turbulent, polluted, and frozen water would not reveal the trees.

questions.passage: The new policy is ______ to everyone: it applies the same rules to every employee regardless of title.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Applying the same rules to everyone regardless of rank is what makes a policy fair. Strict describes severity rather than even-handedness, and confusing or temporary do not follow from the description.

questions.passage: The witness's account was ______ by the security footage, which showed events unfolding exactly as she had described them.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Footage matching the account exactly confirms it: corroborated. Contradicted and complicated would require a mismatch, and anticipated makes no sense for footage.

questions.passage: Some readers found the novel's ending ______, since it resolves none of the questions raised in the first chapter.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: An ending that resolves nothing leaves readers unsatisfied. Satisfying is the opposite, and predictable or lengthy do not follow from a lack of resolution.

questions.passage: Bats are not blind. Most species see about as well as humans do, and fruit bats in particular have excellent vision. The persistent myth may come from the fact that many bats hunt at night, when eyesight is of limited use and echolocation takes over.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the main purpose of the text?
choices: To correct a common misconception about bats
To explain in detail how echolocation works
To compare the vision of fruit bats with that of other bats
To argue that bats deserve greater protection
questions.explanation: The text opens by denying a belief, supports the denial, and then explains where the belief came from; the whole passage exists to correct the misconception. Echolocation is mentioned only in passing (B), the fruit-bat detail is one example (C), and protection is never raised (D).

questions.passage: Consider the humble zipper. Patented in 1913, it was at first used mainly on boots and tobacco pouches; clothing makers were slow to adopt it, and it took a 1930s marketing campaign aimed at children's clothing, promoting self-reliance in dressing, to make it common.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the first sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It introduces the subject in a way that invites the reader to reconsider an ordinary object.
It states the author's central argument.
It summarizes the history that the rest of the text describes.
It presents a view that the rest of the text argues against.
questions.explanation: "Consider the humble zipper" is an invitation to look freshly at something ordinary; the history then follows. The sentence makes no argument (B), contains no summary (C), and is not a view to be refuted (D).

questions.passage: The photographer Dora Maar is often remembered chiefly as Picasso's companion. That framing does her a disservice. Before she met him, Maar had already built a reputation for surreal photomontages and unflinching street photography, and she continued to exhibit her own work for decades afterward.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It presents a common view of its subject and then argues against that view with evidence.
It lists Maar's works in chronological order.
It compares Maar's photography with Picasso's painting.
It describes a problem and then proposes a solution.
questions.explanation: Sentence one states the common view, sentence two rejects it, and sentence three gives the evidence. No chronological list (B), no comparison with Picasso's painting (C), and no solution is proposed (D).

questions.passage: The experiment's result was clear enough: plants exposed to the sound of running water grew their roots toward the speaker. What the result means is less clear. It may show that roots can sense vibration, or it may reflect some subtle moisture difference near the speaker that the researchers did not control for.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It offers two possible explanations for a result whose interpretation the previous sentence called uncertain.
It restates the experiment's result in different words.
It rejects the experiment's methods entirely.
It describes how the experiment was designed.
questions.explanation: Sentence two says the meaning is unclear; sentence three lays out the two candidate meanings. It does not restate the result (B), it raises a possible flaw without rejecting the whole method (C), and it does not describe the design (D).

questions.passage: To make a sourdough starter, mix equal weights of flour and water in a jar. Leave it loosely covered at room temperature. Each day, discard half and add fresh flour and water. Within a week, wild yeast will have colonized the mixture, and it will rise predictably.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how to make a sourdough starter
To describe the history of sourdough bread
To argue that homemade bread is healthier than store-bought bread
To compare different strains of yeast
questions.explanation: The text is a sequence of instructions ending in the expected result. It contains no history (B), no health claim (C), and no comparison of yeasts (D).

questions.passage: Glassblowers in ancient Rome could produce vessels thin enough to be nearly transparent, a feat that would not be matched in Europe for more than a thousand years. How they achieved it remains uncertain, because no Roman glassmaking manual survives.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It notes a gap in current knowledge about the achievement described in the first sentence.
It explains the technique the Roman glassblowers used.
It argues that Roman glass has been overrated.
It compares Roman glass with medieval glass.
questions.explanation: The second sentence says how the feat was done is unknown and gives the reason. It explains no technique (B), makes no judgment of the glass (C), and the comparison with later Europe is in the first sentence, not the second (D).

questions.passage: The novel opens with a wedding, but the celebration is rendered almost entirely through what the narrator notices going wrong: the wilting flowers, a guest's forced smile, the groom's glance toward the door. The scene establishes a habit of attention that governs the whole book, in which surface festivity is always shadowed by what is being concealed.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the main purpose of the text?
choices: To analyze how the novel's opening scene establishes its characteristic way of seeing
To summarize the plot of the novel
To criticize the novel for beginning too slowly
To describe what typically happens at a wedding
questions.explanation: The text describes the opening scene and then explains what it establishes for the rest of the book, which is analysis of technique. It summarizes only one scene (B), passes no negative judgment (C), and the wedding is the novel's, not weddings in general (D).

questions.passage: Why do some cities have grid street plans while others sprawl in tangles? Grids usually indicate planning before settlement, often by a government or a company laying out land for sale. Tangled streets typically grew from paths that already existed, following streams, ridges, and property lines.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It poses a question and then answers it by explaining the origins of two patterns.
It argues that grid plans are superior to tangled ones.
It narrates the founding of a particular city.
It ranks cities by their size.
questions.explanation: Question first, then one sentence explaining each pattern. No preference is expressed (B), no particular city is named (C), and size is never mentioned (D).

questions.passage: Coffee was once banned in Mecca, in Ottoman Constantinople, and in parts of Europe, usually on the grounds that coffeehouses encouraged idle talk and political gossip. The bans never lasted. Each time, the drink's popularity overwhelmed the authorities' objections.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe repeated attempts to prohibit coffee and their failure
To explain how coffee is grown and processed
To argue that coffeehouses should be regulated
To compare the popularity of coffee and tea
questions.explanation: The text lists bans, states that they failed, and says why. Cultivation (B), a policy argument (C), and tea (D) never appear.

questions.passage: It is tempting to call the Antikythera mechanism the first computer. The comparison is not absurd: the device used dozens of gears to model the motions of the sun, moon, and planets. But a computer can be reprogrammed, and the mechanism could not. It calculated one thing, beautifully, forever.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the last sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It sharpens the distinction just drawn by summing up what the mechanism could and could not do.
It introduces a new topic for the text to explore.
It concedes that the mechanism was in fact a computer.
It describes how the mechanism was discovered.
questions.explanation: The third sentence draws the line (reprogrammable versus not); the last sentence restates that line memorably: one fixed calculation, done superbly. It introduces nothing new (B), it maintains rather than concedes the distinction (C), and discovery is never mentioned (D).

questions.passage:
Text 1

Advocates of the four-day school week argue that it cuts costs and reduces teacher burnout, and they note that districts adopting it report little change in average test scores.

Text 2

Economist Ravi Shah examined the same districts and found that while average scores did hold steady, scores for the lowest-income students fell, an effect masked by the average.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would Shah (Text 2) most likely respond to the advocates described in Text 1?
choices: By agreeing that test scores were unaffected for every group of students
By pointing out that the averages they cite conceal a decline among some students
By arguing that the four-day week did not actually cut costs
By claiming that teacher burnout increased under the four-day week
questions.explanation: Shah accepts the average but shows it hides a drop for low-income students, which is B. He does not dispute costs (C) or burnout (D), and A is the opposite of his finding.

questions.passage:
Text 1

The revival of vinyl records is usually explained as nostalgia, a longing among older listeners for the music of their youth.

Text 2

Sales data complicate the nostalgia story: buyers under 30 now account for the majority of new vinyl purchases, and most of the best-selling records are recent releases rather than reissues of older albums.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, the author of Text 2 would most likely say that the explanation offered in Text 1 is
choices: fully supported by the sales data.
incomplete, since it cannot account for who is actually buying records and what they buy.
questions.explanation: Text 2's data (young buyers, new releases) do not fit a nostalgia explanation, so the author would call it incomplete: B. A is contradicted, C is not suggested, and D reverses the point (reissues are the minority).

questions.passage:
Text 1

Many gardeners believe that talking to plants helps them grow, and a few studies have reported small effects.

Text 2

Plant biologist Ines Moreau notes that in the studies showing an effect, the plants that were spoken to also received more frequent attention, and that when watering and inspection were held constant, the effect disappeared.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, Moreau (Text 2) would most likely say that the studies cited in Text 1
choices: prove that plants respond to human voices.
failed to separate the effect of speech from the effect of extra care.
used too few plants to be meaningful.
questions.explanation: Moreau's point is that speech and extra attention were confounded, and controlling for care made the effect vanish: B. A is the opposite, and C and D raise objections she does not make.

questions.passage:
Text 1

Some critics argue that superhero films have crowded original stories out of movie theaters.

Text 2

Film historian Maya Lindqvist points out that the number of original films released each year has actually grown; what has changed is that they play in fewer theaters and for shorter runs.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the relationship between the two texts?
choices: Text 2 supports the critics' claim with additional data.
Text 2 qualifies the claim in Text 1 by distinguishing between how many original films are made and how widely they are shown.
Text 2 argues that superhero films are themselves original stories.
Text 2 restates the critics' claim in different words.
questions.explanation: Lindqvist agrees something has changed but relocates it from the number of films to their distribution, which qualifies rather than supports or restates the claim: B.

questions.passage:
Text 1

The Voynich manuscript, a fifteenth-century book in an unknown script, is widely thought to be written in a genuine but undeciphered language, because the statistical patterns of its text resemble those of natural languages.

Text 2

Computer scientist Gordon Rugg has shown that a simple table-and-grille method available in the fifteenth century can generate meaningless text with the same statistical patterns, so the resemblance alone cannot establish that the manuscript says anything at all.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would Rugg (Text 2) most likely respond to the view described in Text 1?
choices: By agreeing that the statistical patterns prove the text is a real language
By arguing that the statistical resemblance is also consistent with meaningless text and so does not settle the question
By claiming to have deciphered the manuscript
By dating the manuscript to a later century
questions.explanation: Rugg does not deny the patterns; he shows they can arise from nonsense, so they cannot decide the question: B. A is the opposite, and C and D are claims he does not make.

questions.passage:
Text 1

Nutritionist Carla Benn recommends breakfast as the most important meal of the day, citing studies that link eating breakfast to a healthier weight.

Text 2

Researcher Oliver Tan notes that those studies are observational and that people who eat breakfast also tend to sleep more and exercise more; in trials that randomly assigned people to eat or skip breakfast, weight did not differ between groups.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, Tan (Text 2) would most likely say that Benn's recommendation
choices: rests on studies that cannot separate breakfast from other healthy habits.
questions.explanation: Tan's objection is that breakfast eaters differ in other ways, and that trials removing those differences found no effect: B. A is contradicted by the trials, and C and D are not suggested.

questions.passage:
Text 1

Urban planner Sofia Reyes argues that adding bike lanes reduces traffic congestion over time.

Text 2

Transportation engineer Dev Patel agrees that bike lanes have real benefits but cautions that on streets where a car lane is removed to make room for one, congestion typically rises for the first year or so before drivers adjust their routes.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the relationship between the two texts?
choices: Patel accepts Reyes's broader point while noting a short-term effect that runs against it.
Patel argues that bike lanes have no benefits.
The two authors agree in every respect.
questions.explanation: Patel says bike lanes have benefits (agreement) but adds a first-year rise in congestion (a qualification): B. A and C overstate the disagreement, and D ignores the caution.

questions.passage:
Text 1

Some scholars maintain that the Iliad was composed by a single poet, pointing to its unified plot and consistent characterization.

Text 2

Classicist Hana Weiss argues that oral poets working within a shared tradition could produce exactly such unity across generations, so the poem's coherence does not by itself require a single author.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, Weiss (Text 2) would most likely say that the evidence cited in Text 1
choices: proves that the poem had multiple authors.
is compatible with more than one account of how the poem was composed.
is irrelevant to the question of authorship.
shows that the poem was written down early.
questions.explanation: Weiss argues that unity could come from one poet or from a tradition, so the evidence does not decide between them: B. She does not claim it proves multiple authors (A) or that it is irrelevant (C), and D is not discussed.

questions.passage: The recipe calls for fresh basil. ______ dried basil can be substituted in a pinch.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The second sentence offers an alternative to the first, a contrast: "However." The other transitions signal consequence, example, or similarity.

questions.passage: The museum extended its hours on Fridays. ______ attendance on that day nearly doubled.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: Doubled attendance is a consequence of longer hours: "As a result." Nevertheless and In contrast signal opposition, and Meanwhile signals simultaneous but unrelated events.

questions.passage: Several factors made the expedition difficult. ______ the team lacked a reliable map of the interior.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The first sentence promises several factors; the second gives the first of them: "For one thing." In conclusion would end rather than begin a list, and the other two signal contrast.

questions.passage: The company promised to cut its emissions in half by 2030. ______ its emissions have risen every year since the pledge.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: Rising emissions run against the pledge, so a contrast is needed, and "to date" fits the time frame: C. Accordingly and For example would present the rise as following from or illustrating the pledge, and Indeed would intensify it.

questions.passage: The study's sample was small and drawn from a single city. ______ its findings should be treated as suggestive rather than conclusive.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
